https://www.politico.eu/article/europes-.text: Elisabeth Braw is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, author of the award-winning “Goodbye Globalization” and a regular columnist for POLITICO. Her new book, “ The Undersea War ,” is out Oct. 8. Plots against defense executives, a series of arson attacks against private companies and warehouses, and explosive drones at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport. Had any of these worked as intended, they would have caused immense damage, not to mention claimed lives. Advertisement Advertisement This is the situation plaguing Europe today, faced as it is with a proliferation of gray-zone attacks. And while a definitive response from the continent is yet to materialize, the bloc has finally started to name and address the hybrid war it’s been pulled into. No, summits and statements won’t thwart attacks, but acknowledgement is famously the first step to recovery. It was only a miracle that saved workers at Leipzig airport when, on Aug. 4, an approaching drone landed poorly and lost its load of explosives. Had things gone to plan, it would have exploded next to a Ukrainian Antonov plane ready for departure, causing immense damage to a busy airport servicing the people and businesses of large parts of Germany. (Investigators later found a second drone laden with military-grade explosives right next to the airport.) But who would want to maim and kill airport users? On Sept. 1, the German government announced it had determined Russia was behind the attack. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster arrive for a news conference at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images Years ago, European governments would have preferred not to publicly attribute such reckless incidents because with attribution comes the need to respond. But this time Germany openly identified the Kremlin as the instigator, showing just how seriously Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is taking the incident. That’s because the failed drone explosion is only the latest in a series of sinister activity of which Germany has been a particular target. Just before the country’s national election in 2025, the exhaust pipes of hundreds of cars were sabotaged across the country, and stickers calling for people to vote for the Greens attached to their windows. While that last touch suggested environmental activists were behind the campaign, the perpetrators were later identified as agents working on Russia’s behalf. Advertisement Advertisement A couple of months earlier, a parcel — which turned out to contain a bomb — caught fire at DHL’s depot at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The perpetrators of this event, too, were later found to be working for Russia. And a few months before that, German authorities uncovered a Russian assassination plot against arms manufacturer Rheinmetall’s CEO. You all know about these cases, not just because I’ve written about them on these pages but because they were so brazen. And Germany is not the only country to see all manner of businesses — and even business executives — targeted by geopolitically linked strikes. The U.K. has been hit by arson, as have Poland, the Czech Republic and other European countries. In September 2025, objects in the skies above airports in Denmark and Norway forced temporary closures. Drones keep appearing around Scottish offshore installations. Numerous Swedish communication masts have sustained suspicious damage. And in the Baltic Sea, there has been a string of suspicious cable and pipeline incidents. The Eagle S oil tanker is escorted by a tugboat to the Port of Kilpilahti in the Gulf of Finland on Dec. 28, 2024. | Vesa Moilanen/Lehtikuva/AFP via Getty Images So far, none of these incidents have caused devastating damage — though a 2024 arson attack subsequently attributed to Russia destroyed Poland’s largest shopping mall. But each attempt costs the affected businesses money. Each piece of sabotaged infrastructure incurs repair costs and operational losses. Each disruption causes delays and further expenses. In fact, most targeted companies have seen their operations disrupted, which means additional financial hits. In the case of the undersea cables struck by anchors, the owners were left with significant repair bills. For power cables, repairs typically run into the tens of millions of euros. Each incident also costs personnel time. Had the Leipzig drones or parcel bombs exploded, the financial losses — and, of course, the human losses — would have been extremely painful. Even a relatively small incident can leave the target facing significant damage: Last month WB Group, a Polish drone-component manufacturer, was subject to an arson attack and incurred losses of at least €3.5 million . Polish prosecutors believe the attack was, again, instigated by Russia. Advertisement Advertisement But when all this happens, who foots the bill? If the companies are lucky, their insurers will. However, standard insurance only covers standard perils. It doesn’t cover war-like acts, which is what geopolitically linked acts of harm amount to. At least that’s what many standard insurers are unsurprisingly contending. And while specialized war insurers do offer coverage for war, doing so involves having to decide what exactly constitutes war-like acts. The most detailed discussion of this fundamental question isn’t taking place at think tanks or universities. They’re taking place in the insurance industry, as vast amounts of money are at stake. And this — rendering European companies’ operations financially unsustainable — may, in fact, be Russia’s objective. Surveillance drone models from WB Group are displayed during MSPO International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images Credit to the German government for convening the Baltic Sea Security Summit in August to accelerate European nations’ response to a discreditable and dangerous form of geopolitical score-settling, and for calling the Kremlin out. Now, how will these subversive attacks on European companies continue to unfold? You will have to find out without me, as this is my farewell as a columnist for POLITICO. It has been an immense pleasure and honor to have your company. Arrivederci! Photograph: Jon D/Alamy Crime Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England Tactics to include GPS tagging for repeat offenders, high street bans and tougher sentences Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent Wed 11 Nov 2026 06.46 EST First published on Wed 11 Nov 2026 06.43 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England will be targeted in a police crackdown on retail crime, with tougher sentences, high street bans and GPS tagging. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said up to 17 police forces would target the repeat offenders in their area, collecting evidence of offences to secure stronger sentences and ensure they face “real consequences”, backed by an extra £2.5m in funding. Tactics will include the expanded use of criminal behaviour orders – where repeat offenders are banned from high streets and town centres – GPS tagging and intensive supervision courts, where perpetrators must attend regular judicial hearings. Those who do not comply or breach conditions will face imprisonment in the most serious cases, and foreign offenders could face deportation. Graphic showing the rise in reported shoplifting crimes since 2014 Mahmood said the government wanted to target people “who are causing so much harm to our communities”. She said: “A small number of offenders commit a disproportionate amount of shop theft. They wreak havoc on our high streets, leave businesses out of pocket and make retail workers scared to go to work.” The government said it wanted to replicate the success of Operation Kelleher, a targeted crackdown on 10 shoplifters in Bromley in 2025 that reduced recorded retail crime in the area by 70%, according to Metropolitan police data. The number of shoplifting offences recorded by police in England and Wales rose to the highest on record in 2024, surpassing half a million offences. Last year there was a 2% decline. The Metropolitan police said 104 repeat offenders were responsible for more than 5,300 shoplifting crimes over the past two years. Simon Roberts, the chief executive of Sainsbury’s, said retail crime was a “national emergency which requires a national response”. He said: “The number of incidents of theft, abuse, aggression and violence happening in stores right across the country has an unacceptable impact every single day. “We now need to see more arrests and prosecutions of those who target UK retailers without fear of consequences and we look forward to working closely with authorities as these measures are put into action.” Former shoplifters have spoken about how drug addiction and mental health problems are one of the main drivers of this type of crime, and charities have called for more funding for support services. The government said the police crackdown would also be tough on the causes of crime by tackling drug and alcohol addiction “to break the cycle”. Revolving Doors, a charity that helps to rehabilitate repeat offenders, said the scheme was a chance to “follow the evidence on what works, combining focused enforcement with sustained support to address the addiction, mental ill health and homelessness that can drive repeat offending. Success should mean fewer repeat offences and safer communities, alongside more people able to recover, contribute and realise their potential.” Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said dealing with the small group of repeat offenders responsible for a disproportionate amount of crime was crucial. “Combining robust enforcement with targeted support to tackle the root causes could make a real difference to our high streets and communities,” she said.
